children: The rupee is under renewed pressure, falling to around Rs 95.7 against the US dollar and extending its decline for a fourth straight session. The currency has been hit by a combination of surging crude oil prices, stronger US Treasury yields, sustained dollar demand and foreign equity outflows.

The immediate trigger is a fresh spike in global oil prices. Brent crude has risen sharply this week and is nearing $110 a barrel as escalating tensions in the Middle East threaten shipping routes and raise concerns about the flow of oil from the region. For India, which imports most of its crude requirements, an extended rise in oil prices could widen the import bill, increase demand for dollars and put further pressure on the rupee.

"The rupee extended its decline against the US dollar, depreciating 60 paise to close at 95.7. The domestic currency remained under pressure amid elevated crude oil prices, persistent foreign equity outflows, and sustained dollar demand from importers," said Devarsh Vakil, Head of Prime Research at HDFC Securities.

The weakness in the rupee is notable because the Reserve Bank of India has also been conducting dollar/rupee sell-buy swaps for a second consecutive day, with much of the activity concentrated in December maturities. "Such operations can drain excess rupee liquidity and support forward premiums, potentially offering some cushion to the currency," said Amit Pabari, MD and CEO of CrForex Advisors.
"These operations help drain surplus rupee liquidity and support forward premiums, which can provide support to the currency. Yet, the rupee continued to depreciate," said Pabari.
The Middle East is the biggest trigger
The latest pressure on the rupee is closely linked to developments in the Middle East, particularly the growing risks around critical shipping corridors.

"Iran-aligned Houthis seized Yemen's port of Mocha and expanded their presence near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most important shipping routes. Until now, markets were largely focused on the Strait of Hormuz. The latest developments raise concerns that disruptions could occur at both gateways that connect Middle Eastern oil supplies to the rest of the world," said Pabari.

Experts say any disruption to major oil routes could push crude prices higher and keep them elevated for longer. That would be particularly uncomfortable for India because higher crude prices translate directly into a larger import bill.
Why higher crude hurts the rupee
Brent crude jumped more than 7.5 percent, briefly touching $109.30 a barrel. A sustained rise in oil prices can put pressure on the rupee through multiple channels.

"For India, which imports the majority of its crude oil requirements, higher oil prices immediately translate into a larger import bill and greater dollar demand. That pressure tends to show up in the rupee very quickly," said Pabari.
Global rate outlook is adding to the pressure

The rupee is also facing headwinds from global monetary policy. Major central banks are signalling that inflation remains a concern, particularly as energy prices rise. The European Central Bank raised interest rates by 25 basis points, taking its deposit rate to 2.5 percent.

"It signalled that inflation could remain above target for an extended period because of ongoing energy-related pressures. In Japan, rising government bond yields ahead of next week's Bank of Japan meeting continue to keep markets alert to the possibility of further policy tightening," added Pabari.

For emerging-market currencies such as the rupee, higher interest rates in developed economies can make dollar- and other developed-market assets relatively more attractive. This can encourage capital flows towards those markets and add pressure to emerging-market currencies.
Strong US inflation data is strengthening the dollar

The US has added another layer of pressure. Producer inflation rose 5.4 percent year-on-year in August, slightly above the 5.3 percent market expectation, while weekly jobless claims came in at 206,000, broadly in line with forecasts.

The data has reinforced expectations that the Federal Reserve could maintain a tighter monetary stance. Markets are now pricing in roughly a 70 percent probability of a 25-basis-point Fed rate hike next week.
Moreover, a stronger dollar typically creates additional pressure on the rupee, particularly when India is simultaneously facing higher crude prices and foreign equity outflows.
